records.title: Chang-Yan-Ning Granules Attenuates Colitis-Associated Intestinal Barrier Damage by Acting on SSTR1 to Suppress Inflammatory Responses.
records.abstract: Chang-Yan-Ning Granules (CYN) is a traditional Chinese herbal formula widely used in the clinical management of ulcerative colitis (UC). However, its molecular mechanisms of action, particularly with respect to intestinal barrier protection, remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to systematically investigate the effects and underlying mechanisms of CYN in colitis, with a focus on identifying its functional molecular targets and bioactive constituents. A dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced acute colitis mouse model was established to evaluate the in vivo efficacy of CYN. Integrated approaches combining RNA sequencing, network pharmacology prediction, chemical profiling, and public database mining were employed to predict candidate targets. Multi-scale in vitro and vivo validation was performed using THP-1 co-cultured intestinal epithelial cells, mouse colonic organoids, and a zebrafish model of UC. Somatostatin receptor 1 (SSTR1) functional validation was conducted via siRNA-mediated knockdown. CYN treatment reduced disease activity index (DAI) scores, partially restored colonic length, preserved colonic crypt architecture, and increased occludin expression in DSS-treated mice. Across the cell co-culture and colonic organoid models, CYN suppressed inflammatory responses and preserved epithelial barrier integrity, as indicated by reduced TNF-α and IL-6 levels and improved expression or junctional distribution of occludin and ZO-1. In zebrafish, CYN reduced intestinal neutrophil accumulation and ameliorated model-associated alterations in goblet cells and intestinal morphology. Transcriptomic and network pharmacology analyses revealed enrichment of inflammation-related pathways and identified SSTR1 as a candidate mediator associated with the protective effects of CYN. Rutin and rosmarinic acid (RA), two blood-absorbed constituents of CYN, exhibited barrier-protective and anti-inflammatory activities. Drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS) and molecular docking analyses provided complementary evidence supporting potential interactions between rutin or RA and SSTR1. The protective effects of CYN and both constituents were markedly attenuated following SSTR1 knockdown. Further pathway analysis revealed reduced MEK phosphorylation following treatment with CYN and its candidate active constituents, whereas no significant changes were detected in ERK, AKT, or STAT3 under the conditions examined. CYN alleviates experimental colitis and preserves intestinal barrier integrity. Rutin and RA were identified as blood-absorbed constituents of CYN, may contribute to its barrier-protective and anti-inflammatory effects. Functional knockdown experiments, together with DARTS and molecular docking analyses, support SSTR1 as a potential mediator associated with the protective effects of CYN and its bioactive constituents, although direct target engagement and the precise causal relationship remain to be established. The observed reduction in MEK phosphorylation suggests a possible association between MEK-related signaling and the protective effects of CYN. These findings provide a basis for further elucidating the pharmacological effects of CYN in UC and highlight the potential relevance of SSTR1-associated signaling to intestinal barrier protection.

records.title: Mechanically tunable and matrix metalloproteinase responsive hyaluronic acid hydrogel for patient-derived colorectal cancer organoid culture.
records.abstract: Patient-derived tumor organoids (PDTOs) provide reliable and high-fidelity in vitro models for investigating the mechanisms underlying cancer development and progression, as well as exploring new therapeutic strategies. However, the establishment and culture of PDTOs largely rely on Matrigel, which possesses an ill-defined composition and non-tunable mechanical properties, thereby hindering the standardization, reproducibility, and clinical translation of organoid technology. In this study, a hyaluronic acid-based hydrogel incorporating cell adhesion sites and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-responsive degradability was designed for colorectal cancer (CRC) organoid culture. The hydrogel exhibited tunable stiffness within the range of 0.15-2.1 kPa and incorporated an MMP2-responsive peptide crosslinker, providing a favorable microenvironment for the growth of CRC organoids. Organoids cultured in the hydrogel retained the expression of key CRC molecular markers. Transcriptomic analysis further demonstrated that hydrogel-cultured organoids exhibited gene expression profiles highly comparable to those of organoids cultured in Matrigel. Furthermore, hydrogel-cultured organoids maintained their sensitivity to chemotherapy drugs. Collectively, this study provides a well-defined and mechanically tunable hydrogel system as a promising alternative to Matrigel for the culture of patient-derived CRC organoids.

records.title: A pH/ROS-responsive TWIST1-targeting nanogel for epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity modulation and combination immunotherapy in lung cancer.
records.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has substantially improved outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), although durable responses remain limited in a large fraction of patients. Increasing evidence links this resistance to epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a cellular program that not only enhances invasiveness but also restricts T-cell access within the tumor microenvironment. By integrating transcriptomic profiles from immunotherapy-resistant lung cancer organoids with The Cancer Genome Atlas Lung Adenocarcinoma cohort (TCGA-LUAD) and independent immunotherapy datasets, we identified twist family bHLH transcription factor 1 (TWIST1) as a central epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-associated factor linked to poor immunotherapeutic response. Tumors with high TWIST1 expression displayed reduced CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration, attenuated cytotoxic immune signatures, and unfavorable clinical outcomes. To interfere with this EMT-associated immune resistance, we developed oxidized hyaluronic acid/oxidized dextran-thioketal nanogels (OO-TK NGs) for the localized delivery of small interfering RNA targeting TWIST1 (siTWIST1), termed siTWIST1@OO-TK NGs. The nanogel was constructed from oxidized hyaluronic acid and oxidized dextran, crosslinked through a thioketal-containing bis-hydrazide linker that undergoes degradation under acidic and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-rich tumor-mimic conditions. This design enabled controlled intracellular release of siTWIST1 in tumor cells. TWIST1 silencing restored E-cadherin expression while reducing Vimentin and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP9) levels, accompanied by diminished proliferation, and migration. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) tumor-bearing mice. Administration of siTWIST1@OO-TK NGs suppressed intratumoral TWIST1 expression, delayed tumor progression, and extended survival. The effect became more pronounced when combined with programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade treatment, which increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and enhanced IFN-γ-related effector activity within tumors. In a lung metastasis model, combination therapy markedly reduced metastatic burden and MMP9 expression, consistent with partial reversal of the EMT-associated markers. These findings support the potential of combining microenvironment-responsive TWIST1-targeted siRNA delivery with PD-1 blockade to concurrently modulate tumor plasticity and antitumor immunity. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Immune checkpoint blockade has reshaped the treatment landscape of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet resistance remains a major clinical obstacle. Increasing evidence suggests that epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) contributes to this resistance by establishing an immune-excluded tumor microenvironment that limits cytotoxic T-cell infiltration and function. In this study, through integrated analyses of immunotherapy-resistant organoid transcriptomes and clinical datasets, we identify TWIST1 as a key regulator linking EMT activation to impaired antitumor immunity and poor response to PD-1 blockade. Based on these findings, we developed a dual-responsive hydrogel nanogel system for tumor-selective delivery of siTWIST1. The nanogel undergoes degradation under acidic and reactive oxygen species-rich conditions characteristic of the tumor microenvironment, enabling controlled intracellular release of siRNA. TWIST1 silencing reversed EMT-associated phenotypes, suppressed tumor invasion and metastasis, and substantially enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of anti-PD-1 treatment in vivo through increased CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and restoration of IFN-γ-associated immune activity.

records.title: Polystyrene nanoplastics induce size-associated intestinal barrier dysfunction and immune activation in human organoid models.
records.abstract: Environmental nanoplastics are emerging pollutants with increasing concern regarding their potential impacts on human intestinal health. However, the interactions between nanoplastics, intestinal epithelial barriers, and mucosal immune responses remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, human intestinal organoids, organoid-derived epithelial monolayers, and dendritic cell (DC) co-culture systems were employed to investigate size-associated differences in the uptake and biological responses induced by polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs; 50 and 500 nm). Confocal imaging revealed significantly greater uptake of 50 nm PS-NPs compared with 500 nm particles, with preferential accumulation observed in Paneth and goblet cells. Chronic exposure to PS-NPs disrupted epithelial homeostasis, altered the expression of junction-associated proteins (CLDN1, TJP3, β-catenin, and MMP7), and increased paracellular permeability in epithelial monolayers. Furthermore, PS-NP-exposed epithelial models promoted DC migration, maturation, cytokine secretion, and endocytic activity, indicating activation of mucosal immune responses. Mechanistic analysis indicated that NF-κB signaling was involved in PS-NP-associated immune responses, as pharmacological inhibition with andrographolide partially attenuated these effects. These findings demonstrate that differently sized polystyrene nanoplastics induce distinct biological responses, with smaller particles showing greater accumulation and stronger effects on intestinal epithelial-immune homeostasis under equal mass exposure conditions. Our study provides insights into nanoplastic-associated intestinal effects and highlights the value of human organoid-based models for evaluating potential nanoplastic hazards.

records.title: Inkjet-printed single cell-derived pancreatic cancer organoid for intratumoral heterogeneity quantification.
records.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits extensive intratumoral heterogeneity that contributes to therapeutic resistance and disease recurrence. However, conventional bulk analyses often obscure the molecular and functional diversity of individual tumor cell populations, limiting the identification of rare drug-resistant populations. Here, we present a high-resolution, drop-on-demand inkjet bioprinting platform for generating single cell-derived PDAC organoids to systematically investigate clonal heterogeneity. Using this platform, we generated over 600 organoids and characterized substantial variations in morphology, growth kinetics, protein expression, and chemotherapeutic responses. Transcriptomic profiling of 30 individual organoids further revealed pronounced molecular heterogeneity, even among organoids assigned to the same morphological subtype. Notably, morphology-based classification into classical and basal-like subtypes did not consistently correspond to transcriptomic signatures, demonstrating that morphological similarity does not necessarily reflect molecular similarity. Furthermore, individual organoids exhibited heterogeneous responses to gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, including highly resistant organoids whose responses were obscured by subtype-averaged analyses. Together, these findings establish an inkjet-based clonal organoid platform that integrates controlled single-cell deposition with molecular profiling and longitudinal drug-response analysis, enabling systematic characterization of morphological, molecular, and functional heterogeneity at the individual organoid level.

records.title: Dissecting tumor antigen presentation in colon cancer using orthotopic organoid transplantation.
records.abstract: Genetically defined organoids combined with orthotopic transplantation allow tumor-cell-intrinsic alterations to be studied within an immunocompetent, organ-specific microenvironment. We established a murine orthotopic colorectal cancer organoid model for longitudinal analysis of tumor growth and tumor-specific T‑cell responses. Murine colonic organoids were modified by deletion of Apc, Trp53, and Tgfbr2 as well as expression of oncogenic Kras p.G12D. In addition, ovalbumin (OVA) was introduced as a defined model antigen. Organoids were injected into the rectal submucosa of syngeneic mice and followed by small animal endoscopy. Tumors were analyzed histologically and immunologically. Orthotopic tumors developed in the majority of transplanted mice and showed invasive, predominantly gland-forming adenocarcinoma morphology with deep infiltration of the rectal wall. Ovalbumin expression was associated with increased intratumoral CD8+ T‑cell infiltration. H‑2Kb-SIINFEKL multimer staining identified OVA-specific CD8+ T cells predominantly within the tumors, at a lower frequency in tumor-draining lymph nodes, and only in isolation in the spleen. The model allows defined tumor cell alterations to be combined with longitudinal tumor monitoring and analysis of local antigen-specific immune responses in an immunocompetent host.

records.title: FeDx-SF@βE assembly for AML treatment via GATA1/SLC40A1 pathway-mediated iron homeostasis disorder.
records.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive hematologic malignancy characterized by rapid progression, therapeutic resistance, and poor prognosis. Inducing ferroptosis in AML cells represents a promising therapeutic strategy. In this study, transcriptomic analyses first revealed that ferroptosis-associated transcriptional states were closely associated with prognosis and ex vivo drug-response heterogeneity in AML, providing a rationale for ferroptosis-oriented therapeutic design. Based on these findings, and further supported by a transcriptome-based target-scoring strategy, β-elemene (βE), a clinically used natural compound derived from traditional Chinese medicine, was selected as a candidate ferroptosis-related agent. We subsequently developed a nanodelivery system, designated FeDx-SF@βE, based on alcohol-induced silk fibroin (SF) folding to co-deliver ferric dextran (FeDx) and βE. The resulting nanoparticles exhibited a uniform particle size of 182.3 nm, favorable colloidal stability, and sustained drug release behavior. In vitro studies demonstrated efficient cellular uptake of FeDx-SF@βE by AML cells, leading to significantly inhibited cell viability. Pharmacological cell-death inhibitor rescue experiments showed that ferrostatin-1 produced the most pronounced protective effect, indicating that FeDx-SF@βE-induced AML cell death was predominantly ferroptosis-dependent. Mechanistically, βE-containing treatment suppressed the nuclear translocation of the transcription factor GATA1 and downregulated the iron efflux channel SLC40A1. GATA1/SLC40A1 gain- and loss-of-function analyses further demonstrated that activation of this axis attenuated FeDx-SF@βE-induced iron overload and ferroptotic injury, whereas suppression of this axis promoted intracellular iron retention, oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and mitochondrial damage. In combination with FeDx-derived iron supply, βE-mediated inhibition of the GATA1/SLC40A1 iron-export axis resulted in intracellular iron overload, glutathione depletion, ROS accumulation, extensive lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis. Bulk transcriptomic and virtual-cell analyses further supported the involvement of the GATA1/SLC40A1 axis in ferroptosis-associated AML states and linked βE-related transcriptional programs to this regulatory mechanism. In a disseminated AML xenograft model, FeDx-SF@βE exhibited enhanced antileukemic efficacy and favorable biosafety. Collectively, this work provides a combined ferroptosis-oriented nanotherapeutic strategy for AML treatment and highlights the GATA1/SLC40A1 iron-homeostasis axis as a functionally relevant mechanism for ferroptosis-targeted nanomedicine design.

records.title: scREFINE: Label-efficient refinement of frozen scGPT embeddings for single-cell RNA-seq clustering.
records.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) clustering remains challenging because of high dimensionality, sparsity, technical noise, and limited cell annotations. Here, we propose scREFINE, a label-efficient semi-supervised clustering framework that adapts pretrained single-cell foundation-model embeddings for accurate cell clustering. scREFINE uses a lightweight refinement head to map cells into a task-specific clustering space using only 5% labeled cells, while treating the remaining cells as unlabeled during training. To exploit information from unlabeled cells, scREFINE introduces stability-aware soft structural regularization over local neighborhoods, which leverages reliable cell-cell relations as auxiliary guidance without relying on hard pseudo-label constraints. Experiments on five benchmark scRNA-seq datasets show that scREFINE achieves the best ARI on every dataset against every baseline under an identical, leakage-free protocol (mean ± SD over four seeds). A paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the five per-dataset means yields p=0.0625, above the conventional 0.05 threshold because only five datasets are available; we therefore interpret the consistent improvements as strong empirical evidence rather than a statistically conclusive demonstration. A common-embedding comparison confirms that these gains arise from task-specific refinement rather than the pretrained representation alone: adapted baselines receiving identical embeddings achieve 0.00-0.61 ARI, compared with 0.73-0.89 for scREFINE. Ablation analyses further demonstrate that task-specific embedding refinement is the primary driver of improvement, whereas soft structural regularization provides dataset-dependent auxiliary gains and degrades more gracefully than hard pseudo-labels when supervision is scarce. Biological marker-gene analysis confirms that the predicted clusters correspond to canonical cell populations.

records.title: Virtual metrology for process perturbation prediction in lithographic alignment marks using a physics-guided directed attention network.
records.abstract: Process perturbations in lithographic alignment marks deform multilayer profiles, break mark symmetry, and introduce alignment position uncertainty. Although alignment position deviation (APD) and wafer quality (WQ) responses contain process-dependent information, retrieving the underlying perturbations remains challenging because the inverse relationship is nonlinear and strongly coupled. We formulate this task as alignment mark virtual metrology, in which process perturbation values are estimated from paired APD/WQ response matrices. To solve this inverse problem, we propose a physics-guided directed attention network (PG-DAN). PG-DAN uses diffraction limit masked attention (DLMA) to inject wavelength, diffraction order, propagation, locality, and identity priors into APD/WQ attention logits, enabling the model to use physically meaningful token relations rather than unconstrained data correlations. A directed decoder further follows multilayer coupling during prediction. Evaluated on a rigorous coupled wave analysis (RCWA) dataset, PG-DAN achieves a mean R2 of 0.999875, a mean range-normalized RMSE of 0.34%, and a mean range-normalized MAE of 0.23%, with lower estimation errors than conventional neural inverse models. These results support physics-guided inverse modeling for alignment mark process perturbation estimation.

records.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS.
records.abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

records.title: MultiFlow: coupled flow matching for predicting single-cell multiomic perturbation responses in unseen cellular contexts.
records.abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbation requires resolving coordinated changes across molecular layers, yet most single-cell perturbation models focus on transcriptional responses alone. Here we present MultiFlow, a coupled flow-matching framework that unifies generation and perturbation prediction of paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Through bidirectional information exchange between RNA and ATAC generative flows, MultiFlow learns how their joint distribution depends on cellular context and perturbation identity. Across multiomic generation benchmarks, MultiFlow accurately reproduced paired RNA-ATAC states and their population distributions. In multiome perturbation benchmarks, MultiFlow achieved the strongest overall performance in predicting both gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility perturbation responses, outperforming modality-specific perturbation-prediction methods in cell types whose perturbed states were withheld from training. Joint multiomic modeling further preserved perturbation-induced coordination between modalities, including concordant peak-gene effects and cross-modal cellular neighborhood structure. These results establish MultiFlow as a unified generative framework for modeling paired molecular states and predicting their coordinated perturbation responses across cellular contexts. Code and tutorial of MultiFlow are available at https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.

records.title: Prediction transfer does not imply reliability transfer in single-cell foundation models.
records.abstract: Single-cell foundation models are increasingly transferred across tissues, diseases, perturbation screens, and experimental platforms. Although substantial effort has focused on prediction transfer, it remains unclear whether a model's assessment of its own reliability transfers similarly across biological contexts. Here we define reliability transfer as the ability to transfer an accurate assessment of when model predictions are likely to be correct or incorrect and investigate its behavior across ten perturbation-prediction systems spanning multiple datasets, models, and evaluation settings. We find that reliability transfer varies substantially across source-target pairs and cannot be inferred from predictive performance alone, indicating that prediction transfer and reliability transfer constitute distinct forms of generalization. Analyses of biological annotations, network connectivity, target exposure, and contextual factors reveal that prediction reliability is associated with both shared and context-dependent signals, with their relative importance differing across systems. To characterize this variability, we introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints, context-level signatures derived from strictly cross-fitted SHAP explanations that summarize how reliability estimators combine biological and contextual information when assigning confidence. Across systems, contexts with similar attribution-magnitude fingerprints tended to transfer reliability more successfully, and fingerprint similarity identified transfer sources achieving higher reliability-transfer performance within the observed candidate set. However, these relationships weakened under stricter cross-family transfer settings, indicating that transferable reliability structure remains partly dependent on shared contextual information. Finally, transferred reliability estimators produced different perturbation rankings despite identical perturbation predictions, illustrating a practical consequence of reliability transfer for downstream prioritization. Together, these results establish reliability transfer as a distinct aspect of foundation-model generalization and introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints as a framework for characterizing transferable reliability structure across biological contexts.

records.title: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity switches: Molecular design, pharmacology, and therapeutic considerations.
records.abstract: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems are chemogenetic tools that utilize small molecules to regulate protein association, higher-order assembly, and dissociation. Over the past three decades, an expanding repertoire of these systems has transformed the study of protein function and cellular signaling by enabling rapid, reversible, and tunable manipulation of protein localization, assembly, activity, and downstream physiological processes. As these technologies advance from experimental tools toward therapeutic applications, their translational potential depends not only on molecular switch performance but also on the properties of the chemical inducer and engineered protein components. In this review, we summarize the major classes and design principles of representative genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems, with particular emphasis on the pharmacological determinants that define their therapeutic operating window, including pharmacodynamic orthogonality, pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, endogenous target engagement, and clinical readiness. We also examine how the biological origin and engineering of the chemogenetic modules influence immunogenicity and long-term compatibility. We further discuss exemplary applications, including pharmacological control of CAR-T cell activity, programmed cell death, CRISPR-based genome and epigenome engineering, and on-demand secretion of therapeutic proteins. Finally, we consider the delivery and coordinated expression of chemically regulated protein components as major remaining barriers to therapeutic implementation and highlight clinically compatible inducers, compact and minimally immunogenic protein modules, de novo protein design, and advances in viral and nonviral delivery as promising directions toward more reliable and pharmacologically tractable chemically controlled therapies.

records.title: Chemical Biology in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: From Ligand Discovery to Virtual Cells.
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how scientists, including chemical biologists, conduct research. This review is intended to serve as an introduction for chemical biologists to applications of artificial intelligence in chemical biology. We review how chemical and biological data are featurized, the types of models commonly used in chemical biology applications, challenges in assessing accuracy of artificial intelligence models, and recent developments in agentic artificial intelligence for autonomous research. The applications we will cover include protein structure prediction, ligand discovery, peptide and protein design, prediction of mutational effects, interactomics and gene regulation, and virtual cells.

records.title: An AI-designed, recombinantly produced FtsZ-directed peptide with in vitro activity against pan-drug-resistant clinical isolates.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is outpacing the antibiotic pipeline, yet antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) - the most-cited alternative class - remain constrained by proteolytic instability, host toxicity, and the cost of solid-phase synthesis. We report an integrated design-to-validation pipeline that addresses these constraints and yields a de novo peptide directed at an intracellular, non-lytic target. Instead of relying on membrane disruption, the design was directed at FtsZ, the essential bacterial cell-division GTPase, at a consensus epitope (residues 60-145) that our alignments show is substantially more conserved across the Gram-positive/Gram-negative divide than FtsZ overall (68.6% versus 50.1% identity between Enterococcus and Klebsiella orthologues) while sharing only approximately 8-24% identity with human tubulin. A sequence-space diffusion model conditioned on the amino-acid composition of experimentally validated AMPs generated ten binders; fusion to 120 cell-penetrating motifs, machine-learning triage, co-folding and replicated molecular dynamics identified a single lead, Combined111. Rather than chemical synthesis, the peptide was produced biologically: the codon-optimised gene was cloned in-house into pHT254 and expressed as an intracellular, C-terminal 8xHis-tagged product in the protease-deficient Bacillus subtilis WB800N host, giving a mean transcript induction of 3.40-fold (SD 2.01, n = 4 biological replicates) and a single band of approximately 11.1 kDa after one-step Ni-NTA purification. Against one pan-drug-resistant clinical isolate of each of seven species, the purified peptide produced larger inhibition zones than a panel of last-resort antibiotics for five of the seven, by a mean of 4.81 mm, although this difference was not statistically significant (95% CI -0.64 to 10.27; t(6) = 2.16, p = 0.074, Cohen's dz = 0.82). Each zone value is a single measurement, so reproducibility was not assessed, and inhibition-zone diameters are not a direct measure of comparative potency. The advantage was consistent in direction but not uniform, the pan-drug-resistant Enterococcus faecalis isolate being the least susceptible. E. faecium FtsZ was the sequence used for the computational design, whereas the Gram-positive organism available for experimental testing was E. faecalis. These findings show that generative design can be coupled to low-cost bacterial expression in one laboratory. FtsZ-directed inhibition is presented here as a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism: target engagement was inferred from alignment, co-folding and molecular dynamics, and no direct binding measurement, FtsZ polymerisation or GTPase assay, or Z-ring localisation experiment was performed. Minimum inhibitory concentrations, resistance selection, haemolysis, mammalian cytotoxicity, and in vivo efficacy all remain to be established.

records.title: PRIZM: combining low-N data and zero-shot models to design enhanced protein variants.
records.abstract: Machine learning has repeatedly shown the ability to accelerate protein engineering, but many approaches demand large amounts of robust, high-quality training data as well as substantial computational expertise. While large pre-trained models can function as zero-shot proxies for predicting variant effects, selecting the best model for a given protein property is often non-trivial. Here, we introduce Protein Ranking using Informed Zero-shot Modelling (PRIZM), a two-phase workflow that first uses a high-quality low-N dataset to identify the most suitable pre-trained zero-shot model for a target protein property and then applies that model to rank and prioritize an in silico variant library for experimental testing. Across diverse benchmark datasets spanning multiple protein properties, PRIZM reliably separated low- from high-performing models using datasets of ∼20 labelled variants. We further demonstrate PRIZM in enzyme engineering case studies targeting sucrose synthase thermostability and glycosyltransferase activity, where PRIZM-guided selection identified improved variants, including gains of ∼3°C in apparent melting temperature and ∼20% higher relative activity. PRIZM provides an accessible, data-efficient route to leverage foundation models for protein design while requiring minimal experimental data. PRIZM is publicly available via Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23035983, and the PRIZM GitHub repository https://github.com/daha-la/PRIZM.

records.title: Tuned Fitness Landscapes for Benchmarking Model-Guided Protein Design.
records.abstract: Machine learning-guided directed evolution (MLDE) is an emerging paradigm of protein design where ML models trained on experimental data are used to guide exploration of a protein fitness landscape. Building an MLDE pipeline involves many design choices across the design-build-test-learn loop ranging from data collection strategies to modeling. The cost of collecting experimental data makes benchmarking every component of these pipelines prohibitively difficult, necessitating the development of synthetic landscapes. In this work, we develop a framework called SLIP ("Synthetic Landscape Inference for Proteins") for constructing synthetic landscapes with tunable difficulty based on Potts models. This framework can be extended to any protein family for which there is a sequence alignment. We show that our tuning framework provides landscapes sufficiently challenging to benchmark MLDE pipelines. SLIP is open-source and is available at https://github.com/google-research/slip.

records.title: AI-Assisted Molecular Structure Prediction from Tandem Mass Spectra: Reliability and Validation.
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has broadened the interpretation of tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) beyond experimental library matching, enabling molecular fingerprint prediction, candidate ranking, and generation of previously unlisted structures. Yet these outputs do not all support the same claim about chemical identity. This review briefly summarizes database-restricted retrieval, database-free generation, and scaffold-guided hybrid methods, and then asks what additional evidence is needed to turn a plausible structure into a defensible annotation. We examine failure modes involving incomplete candidate spaces, erroneous precursor assignments, structurally related isomers, leakage between training and test data, and misinterpreted confidence scores. The review contributes two practical elements: a candidate-discrimination workflow, in which alternative structures are retained and targeted measurements such as multienergy fragmentation, retention behavior, ion mobility, and authentic standards are selected according to the unresolved structural question; and an evidence-to-claim checklist that links each question to the most informative measurement and to the strongest supportable identification confidence level. Both synthesize established analytical principles for small-molecule electrospray LC-HRMS/MS rather than constituting a validated scoring algorithm. By making the basis of each annotation transparent, they are intended to improve the practical value of AI-assisted MS/MS in metabolomics, pharmaceutical analysis, environmental screening, and forensic toxicology.

records.title: [Current Status and Future Perspectives of Companion Diagnostics in Japan].
records.abstract: Companion diagnostics are in vitro diagnostic medical devices used to improve the efficacy or safety of specific therapeutic drugs and play an important role in appropriate patient selection and treatment decision-making. Companion diagnostics are used to select patients in clinical trials of their corresponding therapeutic drugs and are developed and approved in conjunction with those drugs; therefore, in principle, they have been used only in combination with the corresponding therapeutic drugs. In recent years, advances in the development of molecularly targeted therapies have led to the approval of multiple combinations of therapeutic drugs and companion diagnostics for diseases caused by the same genetic alteration. As a result, a test result obtained with a specific companion diagnostic can be used to select patients for treatment with the corresponding therapeutic drug, but not for treatment with other therapeutic drugs targeting the same genetic alteration. To address this issue, in Japan, a regulatory framework for drug-agnostic companion diagnostics has been introduced. Under this framework, companion diagnostics for which the interchangeable use of test results is considered scientifically justified based on a comprehensive evaluation of their analytical performance, clinical utility, and other relevant factors can be used to select patients for treatment with multiple therapeutic drugs. This review provides an overview of the approval status of companion diagnostics in Japan and discusses the background to the introduction of drug-agnostic companion diagnostics, the principles underlying their evaluation, and future challenges.

records.title: [Recent Advances in ctDNA and utDNA Research for Bladder Cancer].
records.abstract: Bladder cancer is characterized by a high recurrence rate and requires long-term surveillance according to each patient's risk profile. Conventional urinary biomarkers including urine cytology, NMP22, and UroVysion FISH have been used to support bladder cancer detection; however, their sensitivity remains limited, particularly in low-grade tumors and in the assessment of minimal residual disease (MRD). Recently, liquid biopsy approaches based on circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and urinary tumor DNA (utDNA) have emerged as promising minimally invasive strategies for monitoring bladder cancer. In these approaches, highly sensitive assays incorporating diverse molecular information, including genomic alterations, DNA methylation patterns, and RNA expression profiles, are being actively developed. In this review, we summarize the fundamental characteristics of ctDNA/utDNA-based liquid biopsy and highlight major clinical studies in both muscle-invasive bladder cancer and non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. We further discuss the current evidence regarding their potential applications in cancer detection, MRD assessment, treatment response monitoring, and recurrence prediction. In addition, we review the potential clinical implications of these biomarkers for personalized surveillance, perioperative treatment strategies, and treatment decision-making, including bladder-sparing approaches. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future perspectives for the implementation of ctDNA/utDNA-based liquid biopsy in routine clinical practice.

records.title: miR-221 and miR-222 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: mechanistic evidence, extracellular vesicle communication, biomarker candidates, and therapeutic prospects.
records.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains difficult to diagnose early and treat effectively. The related microRNAs miR-221 and miR-222 share a seed sequence, but their functions and clinical evidence should be evaluated individually. Pancreatic cancer models support miR-221/222-associated TIMP-2 repression and invasion, miR-222-mediated p57 regulation, and tumor-derived vesicular miR-222 effects on p27 expression and localization. Macrophage-derived extracellular vesicular miR-222-3p has also been implicated in gemcitabine resistance through TSC1-associated signaling. By contrast, the TRPS1-ZEB2 mechanism and the vesicular SPINT1-HGF liver pathway derive from breast and colorectal cancer studies, respectively, and remain extrapolations when discussed in PDAC. Circulating miR-221 has shown exploratory diagnostic associations, but results from general miRNA panels cannot be assigned to miR-221 or miR-222 individually. Tissue prognostic associations likewise do not validate circulating assays. A first-in-human study of the selective inhibitor LNA-i-miR-221 provides early safety and peripheral-blood pharmacodynamic evidence in a mixed advanced-cancer population that included pancreatic cancer; it does not establish PDAC-specific efficacy. Translation requires independent biomarker validation, molecule-specific target-dependence studies, and confirmation of effective pancreatic tumor delivery.

records.title: In Situ Growth of Polyanionic DNA Hydrogel Networks for Nanoconfined Iontronic Analysis of DNA Methylation.
records.abstract: Solid-state nanofluidics offers unique ion transport dynamics for sensitive molecular diagnostics. Herein, we report a nanoconfined iontronic platform for quantifying trace p16 gene methylation (p16-mC) in liquid biopsies. This system couples sequence-specific hybridization with HpaII enzymatic cleavage to strictly eliminate false positives from unmethylated homologues. Genuine target recognition triggers interfacial rolling circle and multiple-primer chain amplifications directly at anodic aluminum oxide nanochannel orifices. This in situ topological growth yields a 3D polyanionic DNA hydrogel that fundamentally remodels the interfacial physicochemical microenvironment. The resulting superhydrophilic transition and localized surface charge accumulation synergistically amplify transmembrane cation conductance, translating subtle epigenetic variations into robust iontronic readouts. Driven by this physical gating, the sensor achieves an ultralow detection limit of ∼33 aM and a dynamic range spanning 10 orders of magnitude. Clinically, the platform effectively discriminates nonsmall cell lung cancer patients from healthy donors using peripheral plasma, demonstrating its clinical feasibility for noninvasive cancer diagnostics.

records.title: Circulating Biomarkers for Interventional Oncology: Current Status and Future Direction.
records.abstract: Biomarkers reflect underlying physiological or pathological processes and support disease detection, cancer diagnosis, treatment selection and prognosis, monitoring of therapeutic response, and identification of disease recurrence in interventional oncology (IO) care. In recent years, liquid biopsy of circulating biomarkers has emerged as a transformative approach in oncology. Given the growing role of IO in cancer care and the potential for circulating biomarkers to directly impact patient care in Interventional Radiology, this narrative review summarizes circulating biomarker types, current detection technologies and workflows, clinical applications in IO care, and next-generation biomarker modalities and detection instruments for Interventional Radiologists.

records.title: Fluctuating Methylation-based ctDNA Detection in NSCLC Surveillance: Implications for Serial Monitoring and Specificity.
records.abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) addresses key limitations of traditional radiographic and tissue-based screening by providing a noninvasive alternative for the surveillance of NSCLC. In our study, we aim to evaluate trends in the performance of a commercially available methylation-based ctDNA test, characterize patient factors associated with fluctuating ctDNA positivity, and evaluate the clinical implications of serial monitoring. This retrospective observational cohort study included patients who underwent lung resection or stereotactic body radiation therapy for NSCLC followed by posttreatment ctDNA testing from 2024 to 2025. The primary outcomes include patient- and tumor-related risk factors associated with ctDNA positivity. A subgroup analysis of the ctDNA-positive group evaluated clinical events and genomic profiling that may influence transient ctDNA positivity. Of the 85 patients studied, 17 (20%) had at least one positive ctDNA test. Both ctDNA-positive and negative groups had similar patient and tumor-related features. Ten (59%) patients with a positive result subsequently tested negative, and 11 (65%) had a ctDNA tumor fraction near the limit of detection (LOD) without radiographic recurrence. No consistent associations were found with timing, adjuvant therapy, inflammatory markers, or tumor genomics. Three patients with ctDNA fractions above the limit of detection had confirmed recurrence; none in the ctDNA-negative group had disease recurrence. Although the utility of serial ctDNA testing is promising for NSCLC surveillance, isolated low-level positivity may not warrant clinical action. We observe frequent low-level, transient ctDNA positivity without radiographic evidence of recurrence, suggesting limitations in assay specificity and need for trend-based interpretation instead of isolated testing.
